questions.q: What is the key difference between an ADR (Lesson 6) and a design document, as described in this lesson?
options: ADRs and design documents are exactly the same artifact with different names
ADRs are always longer than design documents
A design document is circulated BEFORE building starts to help drive the decision itself; an ADR documents a decision AFTER it has already been made
Design documents are only used for AI systems, while ADRs are used for all other software
questions.explain: The design doc's job is to help REACH a decision through review; the ADR's job is to RECORD a decision that has already been reached -- different points in the process.

questions.q: Why does the example design doc include a 'Non-Goals' section?
options: Naming what the design deliberately does NOT attempt to solve prevents reviewers from debating a problem the document never claimed to address, which is a common way reviews stall
Non-Goals sections are purely decorative and have no real effect on review outcomes
Listing non-goals is required by law for all technical documents
Non-Goals describes features that will definitely be built in a future version
questions.explain: Scoping a design explicitly -- what it does and does NOT attempt to solve -- heads off a common source of review derailment: debating a problem the proposal was never meant to address.

questions.q: What is the single most common reason a design doc stalls in review, according to the lesson?
options: Design docs are always approved immediately regardless of content
Design docs are too short to contain enough technical detail

Presenting only one option with no visible alternatives forces reviewers into an all-or-nothing choice, so partial objections have nowhere to go except a full rejection, and the document sits in limbo instead of getting a clean decision
Reviewers never read design documents before meetings
questions.explain: Without alternatives shown, a reviewer with a partial objection can't say 'I prefer this over the alternatives, but address this one risk' -- they're stuck choosing full approval or full rejection, which stalls the decision.

questions.q: What are the three objections every reviewer is implicitly checking for, according to the lesson?
options: What does this cost and who pays for it; what happens when it breaks; and what wasn't considered and why
Whether the document has a table of contents, a cover page, and a conclusion
Whether the proposal uses the most recent industry buzzwords
Who wrote the document; how long did it take to write; and what font was used
questions.explain: Pre-empting cost, failure modes (Risks & Open Questions), and rejected alternatives in the document itself turns the review into a confirmation rather than an interrogation starting from zero.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a 15-page design doc is 'rarely more thorough' than a 3-page one?
options: Page count has a fixed, proven correlation with technical correctness

Excessive length is usually a sign the author hasn't yet figured out the actual decision and is describing everything they know instead of making a specific case, which makes the real decision harder to find
Shorter documents always contain more useful information than longer ones
Longer documents are always objectively better regardless of content
questions.explain: The goal is a clear, efficiently-reached decision -- padding a document with exhaustive detail a reviewer doesn't need obscures the actual proposal rather than strengthening it.
